records.who: MEX/Veracruz de Ignacio de la Llave
records.current_summary:
The record's core practical-safety signal is the worst in the national data: this state led the national LGBT+ fatality count for four consecutive years — in 2021 alone, 10 recorded violent deaths of LGBT+ people, with 19 of 32 jurisdictions recording victims — and closed 2025 with at least 15 recorded hate crimes; the killing of a 27-year-old trans woman, stabbed to death in a motel on 19 November 2025, came after the state observatory had already counted nine hate crimes earlier that year, three of them against trans women, and the Coatzacoalcos-Oluta corridor is named in the national notes as this state's concentration zone. The danger inside the state is metro-and-corridor concentrated rather than uniform.

Legal protections and enforcement are absent in practice: before the 2025 civil-code gender-identity reform — among the last to be legislated — a visitor or resident had no legal route to correct gender documents, and there is no functioning investigation or prosecution machinery, distinct from other jurisdictions where laws exist but enforcement is weak. Activists cite deliberate filing-away of cases, the state prosecutor's office has lost investigative files entirely, and in one emblematic case (a chef killed in February 2021) the homicide file had simply disappeared; the impunity here is total.

prison_adds.title: Trans Rights in Mexico: Progress and Challenges | Human Rights Watch
prison_adds.summary: HRW's state-by-state map of transgender rights in Mexico shows Veracruz was among the last states to legislate: only in 2025 did its congress reform the Civil Code to create an administrative procedure for legal gender recognition, with no age requirement. The page documents no prison-placement rule for Veracruz and no information on where trans prisoners are housed; its Veracruz content concerns identity documents (civil registry) only.

records.current_summary:
In May 2024 the organising brotherhood of a flagship traditional festival in this region circulated a written invitation stating that "men dressed as women will not be admitted"; activists filed a discrimination complaint with the national equality body, and the events are explicitly marketed to foreign tourists - the exclusion is directly visitor-facing.

Newer reporting profiles the region as a fastest-growing tourist paradise and at the same time its most dangerous for the LGBT+ community: several violent incidents are under investigation, in municipalities where armed groups operate, with possible municipal-police participation, and the official answer has been stepped-up visitor security rather than institutional reform.

The legal layer points the other way: the state has allowed legal gender recognition since 2019, extended it to age 12 and above by decree in 2021, and a 2023 Supreme Court ruling fully opened the procedure. A trans visitor therefore stands under a formally protective framework alongside customary exclusion and violent-incident reports at exactly the events tourists attend.

prison_adds.title: World Report 2024: Mexico | Human Rights Watch
prison_adds.summary: HRW World Report 2024, Mexico chapter: documents Mexico's national legal-gender-recognition framework (administrative name/gender-marker changes on birth certificates in 21 of 32 states, a 2019 Supreme Court ruling setting LGR standards, extended to adolescents and children in March 2022). Its SOGI section covers marriage and document-level recognition only and contains no information on where transgender prisoners are housed in Oaxaca or in Mexico generally.

prison_adds.title: Trans Rights in Mexico: Progress and Challenges | Human Rights Watch
prison_adds.summary: HRW's state-by-state map documents that Oaxaca created an administrative legal-gender-recognition procedure in 2019, extended it to children 12 and older in 2021, and saw a June 2023 Supreme Court ruling reopen access for children under 12. As with Veracruz, the page contains no prison-placement data: Oaxaca's only documented gender-identity law concerns identity documents, not where trans inmates are held.

records.current_summary:
Buenos Aires Province carries the strongest sub-national negative signal in the country: the provincial human-rights ombudsman's 2016 submission to the UN Human Rights Committee documents acts of violence, persecution and harassment by provincial police — or by third parties under police cover — against trans and travesti people during operations in three cities (La Plata, Mar del Plata and Esteban Echeverría), under 'preventive policing' frameworks. Academic legal analysis confirms that after the 2012 Gender Identity Law formally decriminalised trans presence, security forces increased use of drug-law prosecution — devolved to provincial justice in 2005 — and street-offence law as the operative instrument of indirect criminalisation of travesti/trans identity: a patterned, state-implicated escalation.

For a trans visitor the operative risk is arbitrary detention during any police stop. The evidence is not a single incident but a documented operational framework that measurably increased police persecution of trans women, and the protective institutions that coexist — the provincial ombudsman's 2024 registry-rectification guide and its discrimination-caseload machinery — are resident-facing and do not offset that exposure. No provincial law criminalises gender identity; enforcement practice, not statute, does the work.

prison_adds.title: Transgender rights in Argentina (Wikipedia) — Prisons section: 2025 women's-prison housing restriction
prison_adds.summary: Wikipedia article 'Transgender rights in Argentina' (rev. 23 Aug 2026), Prisons section: in February 2025, President Javier Milei's government implemented a ban on being housed in a women's prison for trans women convicted of sexual crimes, human trafficking, or any violent crime against a woman. The dated rule is a restriction on women's-prison housing for trans women in specific conviction categories; the article records no other trans-specific housing rule or separate trans unit, implying the operative baseline (for trans women not in those conviction categories) is women's-prison housing. National-level policy; the article contains no Buenos Aires province-specific placement rule.

records.current_summary:
For a trans traveler Bauchi means exposure to a religious criminal code with a capital ceiling: the religious penal code of this state/province remains in force (a June 2025 government note confirms it), and its courts are on record as the place where the ultimate penalty was actually pronounced - in June 2022 a religious court in the town of Ningi sentenced three men, including a 70-year-old, to death by stoning for same-sex acts after a religious-police arrest, the first time the death penalty had actually been imposed for homosexuality in the country. The sentence was pronounced, not carried out: no execution is on record, the accused were released on bail pending appeal, and the June 2025 note records the sentence could not be carried out until ratified by the governor of this state/province.

Practical safety: the moral code is actively enforced - the same government note places a further death-by-stoning sentence for homosexuality from a religious court in this state/province in May 2024, and advisory material in 2025-26 continues to cite corporal enforcement of religious morality law in this state/province. The appellate counterweight exists but is fragile: an upper court quashed two stoning death sentences in 2003, and a monitoring organisation recorded further successful appeals.

prison_adds.title: LGBTQ rights in Nigeria (Wikipedia)
prison_adds.summary: The only Bauchi-specific detention data found in the mandated Wikipedia full-text search plus candidate fetches: the article records that eighteen men were arrested by Bauchi state police and charged with sodomy for dressing as women (illegal under the Shari'a penal code); the charges were later dropped to vagrancy, and the men were held in jail for several years awaiting trial, a pre-trial detention that dissolved by the end of 2011. This documents that persons perceived as trans-feminine in Bauchi have been arrested and held in custody under Shari'a charges for years, but the article contains no information on where such detainees are housed inside custody (male-vs-female wing, special unit, or solitary/segregation), and no trans-specific placement rule, facility or policy is documented for Bauchi.

records.current_summary:
For a trans traveler Sokoto is a statutory-exposure record with verified court-level enforcement: the religious penal code of this state/province took effect on 31 January 2001; male same-sex activity draws death by stoning for married or previously-married offenders and 100 lashes for the unmarried, while acts between women draw a discretionary sentence of up to 100 lashes and/or imprisonment. A June 2025 government note confirms the code remains in force.

Practical safety: a 2019 rights-monitoring study of 173 religious-court cases (2017) covers this state/province among its three sample states/provinces, confirming operational religious courts and religious-police activity here; no capital sentence is on record as imposed in this state/province - that record belongs to a neighbouring state/province - and no trans-specific incident is documented.

prison_adds.title: LGBTQ rights in Nigeria (Wikipedia)
prison_adds.summary: Thin: no usable Sokoto-specific placement finding. The fetched Wikipedia article lists Sokoto among the twelve northern states whose Shari'a criminal codes apply to Muslims (alongside Bauchi, Kano, etc.), with maximum penalties of death-for-men / whipping-and/or-imprisonment-for-women for same-sex acts (per the ILGA citation the article reproduces), and documents cross-dressing criminalization in northern states (e.g., Kano's up-to-one-year prison term for men who dress or behave as women; a northern Islamic court imposing 10 lashes for cross-dressing). This is a criminalisation framework for Sokoto, but the article contains no Sokoto-specific arrest, trial, or custody case, no mention of where trans prisoners are housed, no trans special unit, and no solitary/segregation practice.
